title: URL Shortener REST API
tagline: Build a clean, idiomatic JSON HTTP API in Go that shortens URLs, redirects visitors, and reports click stats.
summary: You'll build a URL shortener as a JSON HTTP API using Go's standard library net/http (with the Go 1.22 method-based mux) or Gin. It exposes endpoints to create short links, redirect from a short code to the original URL, and return per-link statistics, backed first by an in-memory store and then swapped to a persistent one behind an interface. Along the way you'll implement base62 short-code generation, correct HTTP status codes, JSON request/response handling, and table-driven tests — establishing the Go project layout and REST fundamentals the next project builds on.
scenario: LinkNest is a small marketing-tools startup that wants an internal link shortener so the team can turn long campaign URLs into tidy short links, share them in emails and social posts, and see how many times each was clicked. The team is standardizing new services on Go, and as the first backend hire you're asked to ship the shortener as a small, well-structured HTTP service: it must accept a long URL and return a short code, redirect visitors from the short code to the original destination with the right status code, and expose a stats endpoint. Leadership wants the store abstracted so you can start in memory for the demo and swap in a real database later without rewriting the handlers.
learningGoals: Route HTTP requests idiomatically with the Go 1.22 net/http mux (or Gin) using method-and-path patterns
Encode and decode JSON request and response bodies safely with encoding/json
Return correct HTTP status codes for creation, redirection, validation errors, and not-found cases
Generate compact, collision-resistant short codes using base62 encoding
Design a storage interface so an in-memory store can be swapped for a persistent one without touching handlers
Write table-driven unit tests and use httptest to exercise handlers end to end
skillsDemonstrated: Built an idiomatic JSON REST API in Go using the standard library net/http router
Implemented base62 short-code generation with collision handling
Designed a storage abstraction (interface) enabling an in-memory to persistent store swap with no handler changes
Applied correct HTTP semantics: status codes, redirects, content types, and input validation
Authored table-driven tests and httptest-based handler tests for high coverage
Structured a Go service with the cmd/ and internal/ project layout
techStack: net/http (Go 1.22 method-based mux) — or Gin as an alternative
SQLite (via modernc.org/sqlite or mattn/go-sqlite3) for the persistent store
prerequisites: Comfortable writing basic Go: functions, structs, slices, maps, and error handling
Go 1.22+ installed and the go command working on your PATH
Understanding of what an HTTP request/response and JSON look like
Basic command-line usage (curl or an HTTP client like Postman/HTTPie)
Familiarity with running go build, go run, and go test
datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: the core entity is a Link, representing one shortened URL. A Link has code (string, the base62 short code, e.g. "aZ3kT"), long_url (string, the original destination), created_at (timestamp), and click_count (integer, incremented on each redirect). Optionally a Link carries an id (integer, DB primary key) once persisted. A tiny seed set of a few Links is enough to develop against — for example {code: "go1", long_url: "https://go.dev", click_count: 0} and {code: "news", long_url: "https://news.ycombinator.com", click_count: 12}. Stats responses aggregate a single Link's click_count and created_at; you can extend the model with a lightweight ClickEvent (code, timestamp, referer) if you later want per-click history for the stretch goals.
architectureFlow: Client (curl / browser) -> net/http mux (Go 1.22 method+path routes) -> Handler (decode JSON, validate) -> Service (base62 code generation, click counting) -> Store interface -> [in-memory map] or [SQLite] -> JSON response / 302 redirect back to Client

title: Task Manager API: Gin + GORM + Postgres + JWT
tagline: Build the classic portfolio-grade backend: authenticated task management with Gin, GORM, Postgres, and JWT.
summary: You'll build a production-shaped Task Manager REST API in Go using Gin for routing and middleware, GORM with auto-migrations against Postgres for persistence, and JWT for authentication. Users register and log in (passwords hashed with bcrypt), receive a signed token, and then manage their own tasks through protected, ownership-scoped CRUD endpoints with request validation, pagination, and filtering. You'll add structured logging, centralized error handling, config from environment, and go test integration tests that run against a real database — the kind of backend that stands on its own in a portfolio.
scenario: TeamTide is a startup building a lightweight team productivity app, and they need a backend service that lets each user manage a private list of tasks. As the backend engineer you're asked to deliver a secure, multi-user Task Manager API: people must be able to register and log in, and every task operation must be scoped so users only ever see and modify their own tasks. The product team wants clean validation and helpful error messages, pagination and status filtering for long task lists, and enough operational polish — logging, config, health checks, migrations, and tests — that the service can be deployed and iterated on with confidence rather than treated as a throwaway prototype.
learningGoals: Structure a Gin application with grouped routes, middleware, and dependency-injected handlers
Model and persist data with GORM, including relations, auto-migrations, and query scoping
Implement JWT authentication end to end: register, login, bcrypt hashing, token issuance, and an auth middleware
Validate and bind incoming JSON with struct tags and return clear, structured validation errors
Add pagination, filtering, and ownership scoping so list endpoints are safe and performant
Write integration tests with go test that exercise the full HTTP + database stack
skillsDemonstrated: Built a secure, multi-user REST API in Go with Gin, GORM, and Postgres
Implemented JWT authentication with bcrypt password hashing and a token-verifying middleware
Enforced per-user data ownership and authorization on every protected endpoint
Designed paginated, filterable list APIs with request validation and structured error responses
Applied production practices: environment config, structured logging, migrations, and health checks
Authored HTTP + database integration tests with go test for high-confidence coverage
techStack: go-playground/validator (via Gin binding) for request validation
testing + net/http/httptest + testcontainers-go or a Dockerized Postgres for integration tests
prerequisites: Comfortable building a basic Go HTTP service (ideally after the URL Shortener project)
Working knowledge of SQL and relational concepts (tables, primary/foreign keys, joins)
A running PostgreSQL instance or Docker to start one
Understanding of HTTP methods, status codes, and JSON request/response bodies
Familiarity with go modules, go build, and go test
datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: two core entities. A User has id (uint PK), email (unique), password_hash (bcrypt), created_at, and updated_at. A Task has id (uint PK), user_id (FK to User, indexed), title (string, required), description (string, optional), status (enum-like string: todo | in_progress | done), due_date (nullable timestamp), created_at, and updated_at — with a one-to-many relation where a User has many Tasks. Seed data for local dev: one or two users (e.g. alice@teamtide.io, bob@teamtide.io) each owning a handful of tasks across statuses, such as {title: "Write API docs", status: "todo"} and {title: "Ship auth middleware", status: "in_progress", due_date: "2026-07-15"}. GORM auto-migrations create the users and tasks tables from these structs on startup.
architectureFlow: Client -> Gin router -> Middleware chain (request logger -> recovery -> JWT auth on protected groups) -> Handler (bind + validate JSON) -> Service (business rules, ownership checks) -> GORM repository -> Postgres -> structured JSON response back to Client

title: Caching & Rate-Limited API with Redis
tagline: Put Redis in front of a Go service to slash latency, protect it from abuse, and survive traffic spikes.
summary: You already have a REST API in Go; now you will make it fast and resilient by putting Redis in front of it with the go-redis client. You will add cache-aside caching to read-heavy endpoints with sensible TTLs and explicit invalidation on writes, then build a distributed rate-limiter middleware using atomic INCR/EXPIRE (fixed window) and upgrade it to a smoother sliding-window algorithm. You will move session storage out of process memory and into Redis so the API can scale horizontally, protect the cache from stampedes using singleflight and short-lived locks when a hot key expires, and finally instrument everything with a hit-ratio metric and Prometheus counters so you can prove the cache is actually earning its keep. By the end you will have a production-shaped service that stays fast under load, refuses to be hammered, and keeps its state in a shared store instead of a single process.
scenario: TrailBase runs a public product-catalog API in Go that is buckling under load: the product and category endpoints hammer Postgres on every request, a scraper recently took the service down by sending thousands of requests per second, and because sessions live in each instance's memory, users get logged out whenever a request lands on a different replica behind the load balancer. The platform team asks you to introduce Redis as a shared caching and coordination layer so the read-heavy endpoints serve from cache, abusive clients are throttled fairly across all instances, and sessions survive both restarts and horizontal scaling — without ever serving stale data after a product is updated or melting the database when a popular cache key expires.
learningGoals: Implement the cache-aside pattern with go-redis: read-through on cache miss, populate with a TTL, and invalidate on writes
Choose and justify TTLs and invalidation strategies to balance freshness against database load
Build a distributed rate limiter as middleware using atomic Redis INCR/EXPIRE (fixed window) and a sliding-window variant
Move HTTP session state into Redis so the service scales horizontally and survives restarts
Prevent cache stampedes on hot keys using singleflight and short-lived distributed locks
Instrument cache hit ratio and rate-limit rejections with metrics and expose them for scraping
skillsDemonstrated: Integrated Redis into a Go service with the go-redis client, including connection pooling and context-aware calls
Implemented cache-aside caching with TTLs and write-through invalidation to protect a relational database
Built distributed fixed-window and sliding-window rate-limiting middleware backed by Redis atomics
Externalized session storage to Redis to enable stateless, horizontally scalable API instances
Mitigated cache stampede with singleflight request coalescing and lock-based recompute guarding
Instrumented cache hit ratio and throttle metrics with Prometheus and validated behavior under load
techStack: chi or net/http (existing REST API router)
PostgreSQL (backing store from the prior project)
Docker Compose (Redis + Postgres for local dev)
prerequisites: A working Go REST API with read and write endpoints (from the prior REST API project)
Comfort with Go concurrency basics: goroutines, contexts, and the standard net/http server
Basic Redis literacy: keys, TTLs, and common commands (GET/SET/INCR/EXPIRE)
Familiarity with SQL and a relational database as the source of truth
Docker and Docker Compose for running Redis and Postgres locally
datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: reuse the catalog domain from the prior REST API project. The Postgres source of truth holds products (id, sku, name, description, category_id, price_cents, stock, updated_at), categories (id, name, slug), and users (id, email, password_hash, created_at). A seed script inserts roughly 5,000 products across 20 categories plus a handful of demo users so read endpoints have realistic cardinality and a clear 'hot' subset (a few dozen popular products) to exercise cache hits and stampede protection. Redis holds derived, ephemeral state only: cache entries keyed like product:{id} and category:{slug}:products (JSON-serialized, TTL'd), rate-limit counters keyed like ratelimit:{clientKey}:{window}, session records keyed like session:{token} (hash or JSON with user_id and expiry), and stampede locks keyed like lock:product:{id}. A small load-generation script (hey/vegeta or a Go client) drives repeated and bursty traffic against the hot keys.
architectureFlow: Client -> Rate-limit middleware (Redis INCR/EXPIRE per client key) -> [over limit: 429] or [allowed] -> Session middleware (load session:{token} from Redis) -> Handler -> Cache-aside lookup (GET product:{id}) -> [hit: return cached JSON] or [miss: singleflight/lock -> query Postgres -> SET with TTL -> return] -> Write handler (UPDATE Postgres -> DEL/invalidate cache keys) -> Metrics middleware records hit/miss + throttle counters -> /metrics endpoint

title: Real-Time Notifications: WebSockets & SSE
tagline: Build a concurrency-heavy realtime service that pushes live updates over WebSockets, falls back to SSE, and scales across nodes with Redis pub/sub.
summary: You will build a real-time notification service in Go that pushes live updates to thousands of connected clients. Starting from the WebSocket upgrade with gorilla/websocket, you will design a hub/broadcast architecture where a central hub owns a registry of clients and each connection runs dedicated read and write pump goroutines communicating over channels — the canonical Go concurrency pattern for realtime servers. You will add ping/pong keepalive with read deadlines to detect and reap dead connections, then implement a one-way Server-Sent Events endpoint as a graceful fallback for clients that cannot use WebSockets. Finally you will make the service horizontally scalable by wiring Redis pub/sub so a message published on any node fans out to subscribers connected to every other node, and you will stress-test the whole thing for goroutine leaks and correct fan-out under load. This is a deeply concurrent project that forces you to reason carefully about channels, goroutine lifecycles, backpressure, and graceful shutdown.
scenario: PulseBoard is a collaboration app whose users expect instant updates — new comments, presence indicators, and system alerts should appear the moment they happen, without refreshing. Today the frontend polls a REST endpoint every few seconds, which is laggy, wastes bandwidth, and hammers the API. The team wants a dedicated realtime service that maintains persistent connections and pushes events as they occur. It must handle flaky networks (detecting and cleaning up dead connections), support clients behind restrictive proxies that block WebSockets (via an SSE fallback), and — critically — keep working when the service is scaled to several instances behind a load balancer, so a message produced on one node reaches users connected to any node. You are asked to build this service with correct concurrency, no goroutine leaks, and clean graceful shutdown.

Design a hub/broadcast architecture with per-connection read and write pump goroutines coordinated by channels

Build a Server-Sent Events endpoint as a one-way fallback with proper flushing and reconnection support
Scale realtime fan-out horizontally with Redis pub/sub so messages cross instance boundaries
Reason about goroutine lifecycles, backpressure, and graceful shutdown to avoid leaks and deadlocks under load
skillsDemonstrated: Built a production-shaped realtime service in Go using gorilla/websocket and the hub/broadcast pattern
Implemented per-connection read/write pump goroutines coordinated with channels and select
Added ping/pong keepalive and deadline-based detection and cleanup of dead connections
Delivered an SSE fallback endpoint with correct streaming, flushing, and Last-Event-ID reconnection
Scaled fan-out across nodes with Redis pub/sub for cross-instance message delivery
Engineered graceful shutdown and verified the absence of goroutine leaks under concurrent load
techStack: context and sync primitives (channels, context, sync.WaitGroup)
hey / vegeta or a custom Go client for load testing connections
prerequisites: Solid Go concurrency fundamentals: goroutines, channels, select, and context cancellation
Experience building an HTTP server in Go with net/http and middleware

datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: the payload is realtime events rather than a static dataset. A Notification event is a JSON message { id, type (comment|presence|alert|system), channel/topic, payload, ts } where topic scopes delivery (e.g. per document or per user). Clients subscribe to one or more topics on connect. A small publisher — an HTTP admin endpoint plus a load-generator script — emits a controllable stream of events (steady low rate for correctness tests, high burst rate for load and fan-out tests) across a set of demo topics. For horizontal-scaling tests, Redis pub/sub channels named like realtime:{topic} carry events between instances; each app instance subscribes to the relevant channels and relays received messages to its locally connected clients. A seed list of demo topics and a browser test page (or wscat commands) let you connect multiple clients and observe live delivery.
architectureFlow: Client connects -> HTTP handler upgrades to WebSocket (gorilla) OR opens SSE stream -> Connection registers with Hub -> Hub maintains client registry + subscriptions -> Per-connection readPump (reads/handles client msgs, resets read deadline on pong) and writePump (drains send channel, sends pings on ticker) -> Publisher/API emits event -> local Hub broadcast to matching clients AND PUBLISH to Redis realtime:{topic} -> other instances SUBSCRIBE, receive, and broadcast to their local clients -> dead/idle connection detected via missed pong/deadline -> unregister + close + goroutines exit -> graceful shutdown drains and closes all connections

title: Event-Driven Order Pipeline (Kafka/NATS)
tagline: Build an async microservices flow where an order commits state and an event atomically, then downstream services process it exactly once — or compensate when they can't.
summary: You will build an event-driven order pipeline in Go that models the messy reality of distributed systems: services fail, messages get redelivered, and consistency is eventual, not immediate. An order service writes the order row and an outbox event inside a single database transaction (the Transactional Outbox pattern), a relay process polls the outbox and publishes those events to a broker (Kafka or NATS JetStream), and independent consumer services for payment and inventory react to each event idempotently — deduplicating by event key so at-least-once delivery never double-charges or double-reserves. When a step fails unrecoverably, an orchestrated saga issues compensating actions to unwind the work. By the end you will have internalized why you cannot atomically write to a database and a broker, how to make consumers safe under redelivery, and how to reason about eventual consistency instead of pretending distributed transactions exist.
scenario: OrderWorks runs a monolith where placing an order, charging the card, and reserving stock all happen in one big database transaction. It works until the payment provider is slow, and now the whole checkout blocks; worse, a recent 'fire off a Kafka message after committing' hack has started silently losing events whenever the app crashes between the commit and the publish, leaving paid orders with no inventory reserved. The engineering lead asks you to re-architect checkout as decoupled services connected by events. The order service must never lose an event that corresponds to a committed order, consumers must tolerate the broker redelivering the same message, and a failed payment or an out-of-stock item must cleanly roll the order back through compensation rather than leaving it half-done. The business accepts that downstream state will be eventually consistent as long as it always converges and never double-acts.

Implement the Transactional Outbox pattern so state changes and their events are written in one DB transaction

Coordinate a multi-service workflow with a saga and implement compensating transactions for rollback
Reason about eventual consistency: convergence, ordering, and how to observe end-to-end pipeline state

Implemented the Transactional Outbox pattern to eliminate dual-write data loss

techStack: Kafka (segmentio/kafka-go or confluent-kafka-go) OR NATS JetStream (nats.go)

prerequisites: Comfortable building HTTP services and using goroutines/channels in Go
Working knowledge of SQL and transactions (BEGIN/COMMIT, isolation basics)

Familiarity with JSON encoding and struct tags in Go

datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: The system centers on an orders aggregate and the events it emits. Core tables: orders (order_id UUID, customer_id, status enum PENDING/AWAITING_PAYMENT/PAID/RESERVED/CONFIRMED/CANCELLED, total_cents, created_at, updated_at); order_items (order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents); outbox (id bigserial, aggregate_id, event_type e.g. OrderPlaced/PaymentSucceeded/InventoryReserved/OrderCancelled, payload JSONB, created_at, published_at nullable); processed_events (event_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, consumer_name, processed_at) which is the consumer-side inbox for dedup; and inventory (product_id, available_qty, reserved_qty). Seed data provides ~20 products with stock levels (a few deliberately low to force out-of-stock compensation), 5 sample customers, and a seed script that can place a burst of orders including ones designed to fail payment (a customer flagged card_declined) and ones that exceed available stock. Every event payload carries an event_id (UUID), an idempotency/dedup key, the aggregate_id, and a schema version.
architectureFlow: HTTP POST /orders -> Order Service (single DB tx: INSERT order + INSERT outbox row) -> Outbox table -> Relay/Poller reads unpublished rows -> publishes to Broker (Kafka topic / NATS JetStream stream) -> Payment Consumer (dedup via processed_events -> charge -> emit PaymentSucceeded|PaymentFailed) -> Inventory Consumer (dedup -> reserve stock -> emit InventoryReserved|OutOfStock) -> Saga Orchestrator watches events -> on all success: mark order CONFIRMED / on failure: emit compensation events (RefundPayment, ReleaseInventory, CancelOrder) -> order converges to terminal state (eventual consistency)

title: gRPC Microservice Pair — Capstone
tagline: Tie the whole track together: two Go services speaking gRPC behind an HTTP gateway, hardened with deadlines, retries, a circuit breaker, distributed tracing, and one-command Docker deployment.
summary: This capstone brings together everything from the Go backend track into a production-shaped system: two Go microservices that communicate over gRPC with a shared protobuf contract, fronted by an HTTP/JSON API gateway so browsers and curl can reach them. You will define unary and streaming RPCs, propagate context and deadlines end to end so a slow dependency can't hang the whole call, and add real resilience — per-call timeouts, bounded retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker that sheds load when a downstream is unhealthy. You will make the system observable with OpenTelemetry distributed tracing and structured logs that carry a shared trace ID, expose gRPC and HTTP health checks, and implement graceful shutdown so in-flight requests drain on deploy. Finally you will package all of it with multi-stage Docker builds and a docker-compose file that runs the gateway, both services, and the tracing backend with a single command. The result is a portfolio centerpiece that demonstrates you can design contracts, handle failure, and ship an observable, containerized distributed system in Go.

datasetDescription: Domain model & seed data: The system models a simple travel-booking domain across two services. The Catalog service owns products: an in-memory (or SQLite/Postgres-backed) catalog of ~30 offers, each with offer_id, title, location, price_cents, and an availability calendar (date -> remaining_seats). Seed data includes a handful of offers deliberately marked scarce (0-2 seats) to exercise sold-out paths and a few flagged 'flaky' to simulate a slow/failing downstream for resilience testing. The Bookings service owns bookings: booking_id, offer_id, customer_id, seats, status (PENDING/CONFIRMED/REJECTED), created_at. The protobuf messages mirror this: a GetOffer/CheckAvailability unary pair, a StreamAvailability server-streaming RPC that pushes availability updates for an offer, and CreateBooking on the Bookings service which internally calls Catalog to validate. A seed script and a small load-generator script (fire N concurrent bookings, including against scarce and flaky offers) are provided to drive tracing and resilience behavior.
architectureFlow: Client (curl/browser) -> HTTP/JSON API Gateway (edge) -> gRPC call to Bookings Service (with deadline + trace context) -> gRPC call to Catalog Service (CheckAvailability, unary) with per-call timeout + retry + circuit breaker -> Catalog responds or breaker trips (fast fail) -> Bookings decides CONFIRMED/REJECTED -> response propagates back through gateway as JSON; separately Client -> Gateway -> Bookings/Catalog StreamAvailability (server streaming) -> live updates; all hops emit OpenTelemetry spans -> OTLP exporter -> Jaeger (single trace per request); health checks + graceful shutdown wrap every service

milestones.title: Protobuf contract and generated stubs
milestones.goal: Define the service contract in protobuf with both unary and streaming RPCs and generate the Go server/client stubs both services will build against.
tasks: Write catalog.proto with GetOffer and CheckAvailability (unary) and StreamAvailability (server streaming), plus their request/response messages
Write bookings.proto with CreateBooking and GetBooking (unary) messages
Install protoc, protoc-gen-go, and protoc-gen-go-grpc and add a Makefile target to generate Go code from the protos
Generate the stubs into gen/ and confirm the code compiles
Document the contract choices (why streaming for availability, field semantics) in a proto README or comments
acceptanceCriteria: Both .proto files compile and generate *.pb.go and *_grpc.pb.go without errors
The contract includes at least one unary and one server-streaming RPC with well-typed messages
make proto regenerates the stubs reproducibly from a clean checkout
Messages use appropriate types (e.g. int64 cents for money, explicit enums for status)
hints: Version your packages (catalog.v1, bookings.v1) so you can evolve the contract without breaking clients
Pin plugin versions in go.mod (tools.go) so codegen is reproducible across machines and CI
Model money as an integer cents field and status as a proto enum, not a free-form string
milestones.deliverable: Two versioned protobuf contracts with unary and streaming RPCs and reproducibly generated Go stubs.

milestones.title: Implement the two gRPC services
milestones.goal: Build the Catalog and Bookings gRPC servers so Bookings calls Catalog over gRPC to validate a booking, including a working streaming endpoint.
tasks: Implement the Catalog server: GetOffer and CheckAvailability against seeded offers, and StreamAvailability that pushes periodic updates for an offer
Implement the Bookings server: CreateBooking calls the Catalog gRPC client to CheckAvailability, then records CONFIRMED or REJECTED
Wire cmd/catalog and cmd/bookings to start gRPC servers on configurable ports and register the services
Add a Catalog gRPC client inside Bookings and confirm a cross-service CreateBooking call succeeds end to end
Seed scarce offers and verify CreateBooking against a sold-out offer returns REJECTED
acceptanceCriteria: Catalog's unary RPCs return correct data and StreamAvailability delivers a stream of updates to a client
CreateBooking on Bookings makes a real gRPC call to Catalog and reflects availability in the result
A booking against a sold-out offer is REJECTED; a valid one is CONFIRMED
Both services start via their cmd/ mains and register cleanly with the gRPC server
hints: For server streaming, loop sending on the stream with a ticker and return when the client's context is Done
Use grpcurl or a tiny Go client to exercise the RPCs before the gateway exists
Keep the stores behind interfaces so you can later swap in-memory for SQLite/Postgres without touching handlers
milestones.deliverable: Two working gRPC services where Bookings validates via a real gRPC call to Catalog, including a streaming RPC.

milestones.title: HTTP gateway and end-to-end context/deadline propagation
milestones.goal: Expose an HTTP/JSON edge that fronts the gRPC services and ensure context, cancellation, and deadlines flow all the way through.
tasks: Add an HTTP/JSON gateway (grpc-gateway or hand-written handlers) exposing POST /bookings, GET /offers/{id}, and an SSE/streaming route for availability
Attach a request deadline at the gateway and propagate it into the gRPC calls so a slow Catalog cancels the whole chain
Propagate cancellation: when the client disconnects, the in-flight gRPC calls are cancelled (verify no orphaned work)
Add a configurable artificial delay to a 'flaky' offer in Catalog to test deadline behavior
Confirm that exceeding the deadline surfaces as a clean timeout error to the HTTP caller, not a hang
acceptanceCriteria: curl against the gateway drives real gRPC calls to Bookings and Catalog and returns JSON
A deadline set at the gateway is honored across both gRPC hops (a slow Catalog aborts the whole call in time)
Cancelling the HTTP request cancels the downstream gRPC work (observable via logs/context Done)
A deadline exceeded returns a proper timeout status to the caller rather than blocking indefinitely
hints: Always pass the incoming request's context down into gRPC client calls — never context.Background() mid-chain
context.WithTimeout at the edge is the single most important deadline; downstream calls inherit it
gRPC maps context deadline exceeded to codes.DeadlineExceeded — translate that to HTTP 504 at the gateway
milestones.deliverable: An HTTP/JSON gateway fronting the gRPC services with deadlines and cancellation propagating end to end.

milestones.title: Resilience: timeouts, retries, and circuit breaker
milestones.goal: Harden the Bookings-to-Catalog dependency so a slow or failing Catalog degrades gracefully instead of cascading into a full outage.
tasks: Add per-call timeouts on the Catalog client that are tighter than the overall request deadline
Implement a retry interceptor with bounded attempts and exponential backoff for idempotent, retryable errors (e.g. Unavailable)
Wrap the Catalog client in a circuit breaker (sony/gobreaker) that opens after a failure threshold and fast-fails while open
Define a graceful degradation policy: when the breaker is open, return a clear REJECTED/try-later response instead of hanging
Use loadgen against a flaky/slow Catalog and observe retries, breaker opening, fast-fail, and recovery (half-open -> closed)
acceptanceCriteria: Transient Unavailable errors are retried with backoff up to a bounded limit, not infinitely
The circuit breaker opens after the configured failure threshold and fast-fails subsequent calls
While the breaker is open, callers get an immediate, clear degraded response rather than a timeout hang, and retries are only applied to safe/idempotent operations
After Catalog recovers, the breaker transitions half-open then closed and normal service resumes
hints: Layer the patterns: timeout innermost, then retry, then breaker — order matters for how failures are counted
Only retry on codes that are actually retryable (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded on the sub-call), not on InvalidArgument
Tune the breaker to trip before the overall deadline would, so open-circuit fast-fail actually saves latency
milestones.deliverable: A resilient Catalog client with timeouts, bounded retries, and a circuit breaker that prevents cascading failure.

milestones.title: Observability: distributed tracing, structured logs, and health checks
milestones.goal: Make the whole system observable so any request can be traced across services and every log line is correlated by trace ID.
tasks: Set up the OpenTelemetry tracer provider with an OTLP exporter and add Jaeger to docker-compose
Instrument gRPC servers/clients and the HTTP gateway with otel interceptors so a single request produces one connected trace
Inject the trace_id (and span_id) into slog so every log line can be correlated to its trace
Implement gRPC health checks (grpc_health_v1) for both services and an HTTP /healthz on the gateway
Drive load with loadgen and confirm in Jaeger that a booking shows gateway -> bookings -> catalog spans in one trace
acceptanceCriteria: A single CreateBooking request appears in Jaeger as one trace spanning gateway, bookings, and catalog
Every structured log line carries the trace_id so logs and traces can be cross-referenced
Both gRPC services report SERVING via grpc_health_v1 and the gateway exposes a working /healthz
Spans record useful attributes (offer_id, status, retry/breaker events) not just bare timings
hints: Use the otelgrpc and otelhttp instrumentation libraries so context/trace propagation is automatic across hops
Pull the span context out of ctx in your slog handler to attach trace_id to every record
Health checks are what docker-compose and orchestrators poll to decide readiness — wire them before deployment
milestones.deliverable: Full-system observability: one trace per request in Jaeger, trace-correlated logs, and health checks on every service.

milestones.title: Graceful shutdown and one-command Docker deployment
milestones.goal: Package the whole system so it starts with a single command and shuts down cleanly, draining in-flight work on deploy.
tasks: Implement graceful shutdown in every service: catch SIGTERM/SIGINT, stop accepting new requests, drain in-flight, then exit
Use grpc.Server.GracefulStop and http.Server.Shutdown with a bounded shutdown timeout
Write multi-stage Dockerfiles for gateway, bookings, and catalog that produce small static binaries
Write docker-compose.yml wiring the three services plus Jaeger with health-check-based dependencies (depends_on: condition service_healthy)
Verify `docker compose up` brings the whole system healthy, a booking works end to end, and its trace is visible in Jaeger
acceptanceCriteria: Sending SIGTERM to a service drains in-flight requests and exits within the shutdown timeout with no dropped in-flight calls
Each service builds via a multi-stage Dockerfile into a small image (static binary, no build toolchain in the final layer)
docker compose up starts gateway, bookings, catalog, and Jaeger with services gated on health checks, and a booking placed against the stack succeeds
The booking's distributed trace is visible in Jaeger and the README documents the one-command run, endpoints, and how to view a trace
hints: GracefulStop blocks until in-flight RPCs finish; pair it with a context timeout so shutdown can't hang forever
A scratch or distroless final stage keeps images tiny and reduces attack surface
Use depends_on with condition: service_healthy so bookings doesn't start calling catalog before it's ready
milestones.deliverable: A one-command docker-compose deployment of the full traced, resilient system with graceful shutdown on every service.

portfolioTips: As the capstone, this repo should read as your headline project, so invest in the README: open with an architecture diagram showing the HTTP edge, the two gRPC services, and the tracing backend, then a one-command quickstart. The single most persuasive artifact is a screenshot of a Jaeger trace showing gateway -> bookings -> catalog spans for one request — it instantly proves you built a real distributed system, not a toy. Record a short clip of the circuit breaker in action: hammer a flaky Catalog with loadgen and show requests fast-failing then recovering, which demonstrates you understand cascading failure. On your resume, lead with the outcome: 'Built a gRPC microservice system in Go with an HTTP gateway, end-to-end deadline propagation, circuit-breaker resilience, and OpenTelemetry distributed tracing, deployable via one docker-compose command.' In interviews, be ready to whiteboard the timeout/retry/breaker layering and explain context propagation — these are the exact senior backend topics this project lets you speak to from real experience.
